I'll work through both draft chapters carefully, applying each test and the gate test, while respecting all authorized cuts.

---

**Ch 027**

**Candidate 1**: "The idea survived only as art. Adams asked himself whether he knew of any American artist who had ever insisted on the power of sex…"

Source has: "The question…drew him almost violently to study, once it was posed; and on this point Langleys were as useless as though they were Herbert Spencers or dynamos. The idea survived only as art. There one turned as naturally as though the artist were himself a woman."

The draft cuts the transitional setup ("The question…drew him…Langleys were as useless…") and the bridge sentence "There one turned as naturally as though the artist were himself a woman," then jumps straight to Adams examining American artists. The sentence "The idea survived only as art" is a pivot sentence whose logical antecedent (the question about the Virgin/Venus as force in America, and the dismissal of scientists as useless guides) is present in the draft, so the sentence still parses. This is merely less ornamented. **Not a finding.**

**Candidate 2**: "Vaguely seeking a clue, he wandered through the art exhibit, and stopped almost every day before St. Gaudens's General Sherman. Once St. Gaudens took him down to Amiens to see the cathedral."

Source has: "St. Gaudens himself was in Paris… This summer his health was poor and his spirits were low… Adams risked going now and then to the studio on Mont Parnasse to draw him out… and in return St. Gaudens sometimes let Adams go about in his company. Once St. Gaudens took him down to Amiens, with a party of Frenchmen, to see the cathedral."

The draft jumps from "stopped almost every day before St. Gaudens's General Sherman" directly to "Once St. Gaudens took him down to Amiens." The source established that St. Gaudens was in Paris, that they had a regular social arrangement, and that the Amiens trip was part of that arrangement. In the draft, there is no establishment that Adams and St. Gaudens were in contact at all, or that St. Gaudens was in Paris during this period. The sentence "Once St. Gaudens took him down to Amiens" uses a definite prior relationship ("took him") that has no antecedent basis in the draft — the draft only says Adams "stopped before" the Sherman statue, which was a sculpture already on display, not a live interaction. A reader would ask: how did Adams and St. Gaudens come to travel to Amiens together? The social connection that makes this plausible was entirely cut.

Gate test: A competent reader with no source access would be genuinely puzzled — the draft has Adams stopping before a statue, then suddenly St. Gaudens (who has not been placed in Paris or in Adams's company) takes him to Amiens. The leap is a mid-scene jump: definite social relationship ("took him") used without prior establishment in the draft.

**Finding 1** — valid.

**Candidate 3**: Draft Ch 027: "Not until they found themselves studying the sculpture of the western portal did it dawn on Adams's mind that, for his purposes, St. Gaudens on that spot had more interest to him than the cathedral itself. Adams never tired of quoting the supreme phrase of his idol Gibbon, before the Gothic cathedrals: 'I darted a contemptuous look on the stately monuments of superstition.' Gibbon ignored the Virgin, because in 1789 religious monuments were out of fashion. St. Gaudens had passed beyond all."

Source between the Gibbon quote and "St. Gaudens had passed beyond all" has a long discussion of the humor and depth of Gibbon's remark, Ruskin, and "One sees what one brings." The draft cuts this and also cuts the setup "He liked the stately monuments much more than he liked Gibbon **or Ruskin**." The draft retains "he liked Gibbon or Ruskin" in the next sentence, so "Ruskin" appears without prior introduction in the draft. Let me check: "St. Gaudens had passed beyond all. He liked the stately monuments much more than he liked Gibbon or Ruskin." Ruskin is mentioned in the draft but without any prior context, since the source's discussion of Ruskin was cut. Is Ruskin a named figure requiring a gloss, or a well-known enough name that the reader understands the point? Ruskin is a historically well-known figure; the sentence "more than he liked Gibbon or Ruskin" parses without confusion — the reader understands Adams is comparing St. Gaudens's attitude to two famous critics of Gothic architecture. **Not a finding** under the gate test.

**Candidate 4**: Ch 027 draft: "For a symbol of power, St. Gaudens instinctively preferred the horse, as was plain in his horse and Victory of the Sherman monument. The attitude was so American that, for at least forty years, Adams had never realized that any other could be in sound taste. Only since 1895 had he begun to feel the Virgin or Venus as force…"

Source has between these: "How many years had he taken to admit a notion of what Michael Angelo and Rubens were driving at? He could not say; but he knew that only since 1895…" The draft drops the Michelangelo/Rubens sentence and moves directly to "Only since 1895." This is a cut of an explanatory clause; the "Only since 1895" sentence still parses and conveys meaning. **Not a finding.**

**Candidate 5**: Ch 027 draft: "Yet in mind and person St. Gaudens was a survival of the 1500s…" — this whole paragraph is present and intact. No issue.

**Candidate 6**: "Yet in mechanics, both energies acted as interchangeable force on man…"

Source: "Yet in mechanics, whatever the mechanicians might think, both energies acted as interchangeable force on man…" Minor compression, parses fine. **Not a finding.**

---

**Ch 028**

**Candidate 7**: "The Senate took the place of Shakespeare, and offered real Brutuses and Bolingbrokes, Jack Cades, Falstaffs, and Malvolios—endless varieties of human nature nowhere else to be studied… Hay still felt the humor, though more and more rarely… The old friend was lost, and only the teacher remained, driven to madness by the complexities and multiplicities of his new world."

Source: "He was thinking of his friend Blaine, and might have thought of all his predecessors… The Senate took the place of Shakespeare… 'Life is so gay and horrid!' Hay still felt the humor… The old friend was lost…"

The draft has already quoted "Life is so gay and horrid!" earlier (in the treaty/consulate passage), so when the Senate-Shakespeare sentence appears, "Hay still felt the humor" refers back to that earlier quote in the draft — this is coherent. "The old friend was lost" — who is "the old friend"? In the source, this refers to Hay's old personality/wit being displaced by official grimness. In the draft, this phrase appears without the setup of Hay's complaint that the job had "made him a bore." Let me check: the draft has "what he felt most was the enormous complexity and friction of the vast mass he was trying to guide" — then "The old friend was lost, and only the teacher remained." Without the source's sentence "He bitterly complained that it had made him a bore—of all things the most senatorial, and to him the most obnoxious," the referent of "The old friend" is ambiguous. Could mean Hay himself as Adams's friend is being "lost," or could mean Hay's former self. A reader without the source would read "The old friend was lost" and, given the preceding context about Hay's complexity and friction, might reasonably read it as Hay (the friend) being lost to overwork — which is actually a meaning the text supports. The gate test: slightly ambiguous but not genuinely misleading in a damaging way. **Borderline — reject.**

**Candidate 8**: "Already Hay literally staggered in his tracks for weariness. More worn than he, Clarence King dropped. One day in the spring he stopped an hour in Washington to bid good-bye, cheerily and simply telling how his doctors had condemned him to Arizona for his lungs."

"he stopped" — antecedent is "Clarence King" (the immediately preceding subject). In the source this is also "he stopped." This is unambiguous in context. **Not a finding.**

**Candidate 9**: "He had surrendered all his favorite prejudices, and foresworn even the forms of criticism—except for his pet amusement, the Senate, which was a tonic or stimulant necessary to healthy life; he had accepted uniformity and Pteraspis and ice age and tramways and telephones; and now—just when he was ready to hang the crowning garland on the brow of a completed education—science itself warned him to begin it again from the beginning."

"he had accepted uniformity and Pteraspis" — Pteraspis was mentioned in passing ("uniformity and Pteraspis") without the elaborate geological digression. This is an authorized digression removal (Ch 017, Ch 021). The word appears as a residue of an authorized cut. Per the rules, residues of authorized cuts are not findings. **Not a finding.**

**Candidate 10**: "Maundering among the magnets he bethought himself that once, a full generation earlier, he had begun active life by writing a confession of geological faith at the bidding of Sir Charles Lyell. He read it again, and saw his doubts grown larger."

Source: "He read it again, and thought it better than he could do at sixty-three; but elderly minds always work loose. He saw his doubts grown larger, and became curious to know what had been said about them since 1870. The Geological Survey supplied stacks of volumes, and reading for steady months; while, the longer he read, the more he wondered, pondered, doubted what his delightful old friend Sir Charles Lyell would have said about it."

The draft compresses to "He read it again, and saw his doubts grown larger." This is a compressed but parseable sentence. **Not a finding.**

**Candidate 11**: "Seeking some impersonal point for measure, he turned to see what had happened to his oldest friend and cousin the ganoid fish, the Pteraspis of Ludlow and Wenlock, with whom he had sported when geological life was young."

Source at this point has: "as though they had all remained together in time to act the Mask of Comus at Ludlow Castle, and repeat 'how charming is divine philosophy!'" — cut in draft. The draft's sentence still parses cleanly. **Not a finding.**

**Candidate 12**: "In thought the Schools, like the Church, raised ignorance to a faith and degraded dogma to heresy. Evolution survived like the trilobites without evolving, and yet the evolutionists held the whole field. The geologists had submitted sadly to the violence inflicted on them by the Pontiff of Physical Religion, Lord Kelvin, in the effort to force unification of the universe; they had murmured Ignoramus under their breath; but they had never dared to assert the Ignorabimus that lay on the tips of their tongues."

Source between "evolutionists held the whole field" and "The geologists had submitted": "and had even plucked up courage to rebel against the Cossack ukase of Lord Kelvin forbidding them to ask more than twenty million years for their experiments. No doubt the geologists had always submitted sadly to this last and utmost violence…" The draft cuts the setup that explains *what* Kelvin's demand was (20 million years limit), then says "The geologists had submitted sadly to the violence inflicted on them by the Pontiff of Physical Religion, Lord Kelvin, in the effort to force unification of the universe." Without the source's explanation that Kelvin was the "Pontiff of Physical Religion" who had issued a specific time-limit "ukase," the phrase "Pontiff of Physical Religion, Lord Kelvin" appears in the draft. However, the draft *does* call him "the Pontiff of Physical Religion" inline, so it provides its own gloss. The sentence parses. **Not a finding.**

**Candidate 13 (the "broken pivot" check on Ch 028)**: "Adams saw no way out, and laughed at Hay for his helplessness."

Source: "Nine statesmen out of ten, in Europe, accepted this result in advance, seeing no way to prevent it. Adams saw none, and laughed at Hay for his helplessness."

Draft: "Adams saw no way out, and laughed at Hay for his helplessness." The draft restructures this slightly but it reads fine in context. **Not a finding.**
